summary: In this excerpt from a fiction novel, the narrator shows Arthur and Professor Halliday the crumpled pages recovered from Martinez's condo, revealing that Martinez burned Halliday's work and her own because she had proved P equals NP. The narrator explains the P versus NP problem to Arthur, describing P problems as quickly solvable and NP problems as quickly verifiable but not necessarily quickly solvable. Halliday then warns that the proof would threaten the economy and encryption, and would make logistics and protein folding easy.
one_line: In a novel excerpt, the narrator reveals Martinez's proof that P equals NP and explains the problem's stakes to Arthur and Halliday.
key_facts: The narrator pulled crumpled pages from Martinez's condo out of his pocket and handed them to Halliday.
Martinez burned Professor Halliday's work after she burned her own, because she was afraid and had found something.
The narrator states that Martinez proved P equals NP.
The P versus NP problem is a problem in mathematics concerning how difficult problems are computationally.
Problems in the set P can be solved quickly, meaning in polynomial time on a deterministic Turing machine.
Problems in NP can be verified quickly if a solution is available, but may not be quickly solvable.
The narrator uses a maze analogy: checking a maze solution is easy, but finding the solution is much harder.
Mathematics has never proven whether P equals NP, whether they are unequal, or whether the question is unprovable.
Most people figured P did not equal NP before the proof.
Halliday says the proof threatened the economy and could revolutionize logistics and protein folding.
Halliday says encryption works because once you have the code, you have access, so the proof could break it.
